Hertford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Hertfordshire county town
s1loc: Hertford, the county town of Hertfordshire, anchors its visitor economy on Hertford Castle, a Norman fortress and former Royal Palace whose Edward IV gatehouse on Gascoyne Way stands above landscaped grounds open free through the year. Hertford Museum, set in a seventeenth-century townhouse on Bull Plain, tells the local and regimental story, while Parliament Square, Market Place and the timber-framed streets of the old town draw day-trippers across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the rivers, where Hartham Common spreads open riverside meadow beside the Lea for walking, cycling, kayaking and paddleboarding, and Castle Weir marks the head of the Lee Navigation. Panshanger Park, a Grade II-star registered landscape at Hertingfordbury, and the surrounding Mimram and Beane valleys give activity operators and family visitors a broad outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture centre on Hertford Theatre, the reborn Castle Hall venue with its auditorium, studio and gallery, alongside the Grade II-listed Salisbury Arms Hotel traced to 1431 on the run between Parliament Square and Market Place. The old corn mill at Mill Bridge, the River Mimram and the historic quarter around The Wash and Bircherley Green carry a busy events and market calendar through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade led by the Salisbury Arms and McMullen's town-centre houses, with a guide scene built on castle and river tours and the surrounding Hertfordshire countryside. Hertford East and Hertford North stations run direct services to London Liverpool Street and Moorgate, while the A414 and the Lea Valley draw weekend visitors out from Hoddesdon, Welwyn Garden City and Cheshunt across the season.

Totton.region: Totton and the western edge of the New Forest
Totton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy on the edge of the New Forest
s1loc: Totton sits on the western gateway to the New Forest, with Eling Tide Mill its marquee draw, one of very few working tide mills in the country, grinding flour beside Hampshire's only surviving toll bridge across Bartley Water, in use since at least 1418. The historic Eling waterside, its quay and the wider Totton and Eling parish give the town a genuine visitor pull at the head of Southampton Water through the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Testwood Lakes, the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Wildlife Trust nature reserve and education centre with its walking, fishing and bird-watching, while Goatee Beach and the Eling foreshore line the estuary. Close by, Paultons Park with Peppa Pig World, Longdown Activity Farm and the New Forest Wildlife Park at Ashurst keep family operators and activity centres working hard across the season.

Heritage and culture run through the Eling Experience and the old maritime quarter, with the Test Way long-distance path striking north from Totton through Romsey toward Inkpen Beacon, and the open heath, ponies and ancient woodland of the New Forest National Park beginning on the doorstep. The conservation streets of Eling and the Bartley Water crossing carry walkers, anglers and day-trippers through the year.

Underpinning it all is a guesthouse, inn and Bed and Breakfast trade serving the New Forest fringe and the wider Southampton area, with a guide and tour scene built on forest walks and estuary trips. Totton station on the South West Main Line runs direct to London Waterloo, Bournemouth and Southampton Central, while the M27, Southampton Airport and Bluestar buses through Calmore carry visitors from Southampton, Eastleigh and Winchester across the season.

Burntwood.region: Burntwood and the Cannock Chase area
Burntwood.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy on the edge of Cannock Chase
s1loc: Burntwood sits on the northern edge of Cannock Chase, with Chasewater Country Park its marquee draw, a 360-hectare site of heath and water opened in 1797 as the largest canal-feeder reservoir still in use. The Chasewater Railway runs vintage steam and diesel trains alongside the lake from its heritage station, and the Chasewater Innovation Centre handles visitor information, exhibitions and events, pulling day-trippers in across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer is built on the water, with sailing, wakeboarding, water-skiing, paddleboarding and water zorbing on Chasewater, plus nature trails, bird-watching and cycling around its Sites of Special Scientific Interest. Prince's Park at Chase Terrace, the open heath and the wider Cannock Chase National Landscape with its forest trails give activity operators and family visitors a strong outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture run through Christ Church on Church Road, rebuilt in 1819 next to Prince's Park, and the old mining communities of Chase Terrace and Chasetown, the latter home to one of football's oldest grounds. Burntwood Library at Sankey's Corner, the Burntwood Family History Group story and the events calendar at Chasewater carry visitors through the year on the edge of the Chase.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving the Cannock Chase and Lichfield visitor area, with a guide scene built on heathland walks and railway trips. The A5190, A461 and A5 carry day-trippers in, with Lichfield Cathedral, Lichfield City and Trent Valley stations and the wider West Midlands drawing weekend crowds out from Lichfield, Cannock and Walsall across the season.

Farnworth.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Bolton area
s1loc: Farnworth, in the Croal and Irwell valleys south of Bolton, anchors its visitor draw on Moses Gate Country Park, a 750-acre Local Nature Reserve of mill lodges, woodland and reclaimed land along the A6053 toward Little Lever. The Crompton Lodges, the Kingfisher Trail and the riverside paths give the town a substantial green attraction within easy reach of Bolton town centre across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer spreads across the country park, with walking, cycling, fishing and bird-watching around the lodges, and the protected grassland of Nob End, a Site of Special Scientific Interest since 1988. Farnworth Park, a fine Victorian municipal park with its lodge and bandstand, plus the woodland trails toward Darcy Lever and Prestolee, keep families and activity operators working through the season in the Croal and Irwell valleys.

Heritage and culture run through the industrial story of the Farnworth Paper Mills, once among the country's biggest under Thomas Bonsor Crompton, and Rock Hall, the early-nineteenth-century house built by the Crompton family that now serves the park. The Prestolee Aqueduct and Nob End locks on the Manchester, Bolton and Bury Canal carry walkers and heritage visitors through the year along the valley floor.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving the wider Bolton and Manchester visitor area, with a guide scene built on canal towpaths and country-park trails. Moses Gate station runs direct trains toward Manchester Victoria and Bolton, while the A666 St Peter's Way and the local bus network carry day-trippers out from Bolton, Bury and Radcliffe across the season.

Jarrow.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of South Tyneside
s1loc: Jarrow anchors its visitor economy on Jarrow Hall, the Anglo-Saxon Farm, Village and Bede Museum on the former Bede's World site, celebrating the Venerable Bede beside the ruins of St Paul's Monastery where the Codex Amiatinus was written. The Bede Museum's Age of Bede exhibit, the reconstructed Gyrwe farm and the medieval herb garden of the Georgian Jarrow Hall house draw heritage visitors across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the Tyne, with riverside and country trails linking the town toward South Shields and the coast, and the green spaces around St Paul's and the Don. The St Bede's Way and Jarrow-to-Bede walking and cycle routes, plus the wider South Tyneside parks, give families and activity operators a steady outdoor offer through the season on the river's south bank.

Heritage and culture centre on the Jarrow Crusade of 1936, marked by the Spirit of Jarrow bronze group and the steel relief on Bede Metro station, with Jarrow Town Hall on Grange Road built between 1902 and 1904 carrying its commemorative plaque. St Paul's Church and its seventh-century monastic remains, among the most important early Christian sites in England, anchor the events and history calendar through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, inn and guesthouse trade serving the South Tyneside coast and the wider Newcastle area, with a guide scene built on Bede, Saxon and Jarrow March history. Bede and Jarrow Tyne and Wear Metro stations link the town to Newcastle and South Shields, while the Tyne Tunnel's southern portal and the A19 carry visitors out from South Shields, Gateshead and Washington across the season.

Penarth.region: Penarth and the Vale of Glamorgan
Penarth.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Vale of Glamorgan
s1loc: Penarth runs a busy seaside visitor economy built on its Edwardian pier and the Art Deco Penarth Pier Pavilion of 1929 to 1930, whose vaulted gallery, sixty-eight-seat cinema and cafe overlook the Bristol Channel. The Esplanade, the landscaped Italian Gardens and the seafront terraces, with views to Flat Holm and Steep Holm, draw day-trippers and weekend crowds to this Victorian resort across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Cosmeston Lakes Country Park, a hundred-hectare reserve of lakes, meadow and Site of Special Scientific Interest habitat between Penarth and Sully, opened in 1978 with an adventure play area, cafe and watersports facilities. The Kymin, a five-acre wooded estate and garden above Beach Road, and the cliff-top Wales Coast Path give families and activity operators a strong outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture run through the Turner House Gallery, built in 1887 for flour merchant James Pyke Thompson and now part of the National Museum of Wales, and Cosmeston Medieval Village, a reconstructed fourteenth-century settlement within the country park. The Victorian villas and streets above the seafront, the Pier Pavilion's arts programme and the town's festival calendar carry visitors through the year along the Bristol Channel coast.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, inn and guesthouse trade serving the Cardiff and Vale of Glamorgan visitor area, with a guide scene built on pier, coast and country-park tours. Penarth and Dingle Road stations run direct trains into Cardiff Central, while the A4160, the M4 and Cardiff Airport carry day-trippers out from Cardiff, Barry and Caerphilly across the season.

Congleton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of east Cheshire
s1loc: Congleton anchors its visitor economy on Little Moreton Hall, the National Trust's celebrated moated Tudor timber-framed house that has stood for over five hundred years just outside the town, with its costumed Living History team. Congleton Museum, housed in the old police station behind the Town Hall, holds six coin hoards, a medieval log boat and Civil War stories, giving the town a strong heritage draw across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Astbury Mere Country Park, set in a former sand quarry ten minutes from the town centre, with wildflower meadows, lakeside paths and views toward Congleton Edge and Mow Cop. The Victorian Congleton Park of 1871, with its restored jubilee pavilion, bandstand, bowling green and riverside walks along the Dane, gives families and activity operators a steady outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture run through Daneside Theatre, home to the Congleton Musical Theatre Society since 1932, and the Neolithic Bridestones chambered cairn above the town on the flank of Cloud Hill, built around 4,500 years ago. The Congleton Heritage Festival, the textile and bear-baiting history that earned the town its nickname, and the events calendar at Congleton Park carry visitors through the year across east Cheshire.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving the Cheshire and Staffordshire Moorlands visitor area, with a guide scene built on Tudor-hall, country-park and canal trails. Congleton station runs direct trains toward Manchester and Stoke-on-Trent, while the A34, A527 and the Macclesfield Canal carry day-trippers out toward Mow Cop Castle, Biddulph Grange and the towns of Macclesfield, Sandbach and Biddulph across the season.
